body:
Introduction
Membranous nephropathy (MN) of the kidney allograft can represent recurrent,
de novo
, and very rarely, donor-derived disease. Despite its negative impact on allograft survival,
1
our understanding of
de novo
MN has just begun to unfold.
Cumulative evidence suggests that a proportion of
de novo
MN are alloimmune in nature
1
,
2
and that protocadherin FAT1 (FAT1) is likely the target antigen in a subset of
de novo
MN developing in the context of antibody-mediated rejection (ABMR).
3
,
4
However, the temporal relation between FAT1 levels,
de novo
MN, and ABMR has not been studied.
Herein, we present a detailed case of a patient with
de novo
FAT1-associated MN, who was briefly described previously.
3
We specifically focus on glomerular FAT1 levels assessed by spectral counts on mass spectrometry in kidney tissue over time. To further our understanding of this unusual complication, we similarly analyzed serial allograft biopsies from a second patient with
de novo
FAT1-associated MN developing in the context of ABMR and contrasted the findings with 4 cases of ABMR without MN. The key teaching points of this report are presented in
Table 1
.
Table 1
Teaching points
There is apparent association between glomerular FAT1 levels and concurrent antibody-mediated rejection in
de novo
membranous nephropathy of the kidney allograft.
Antibody-mediated rejection without concurrent membranous nephropathy is not associated with FAT1 accumulation.
Alloimmune response may trigger the development of FAT1-associated membranous nephropathy in susceptible patients.
Potential genetic susceptibility for the development of FAT1-associated membranous nephropathy remains unknown.
Case Presentation
A 43-year-old Black male presented with low grade fever and acute kidney failure 4 years after donating a kidney to a sibling carrying the diagnosis of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. Laboratory work-up revealed serum creatinine: 7 mg/dl, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio: 31 g/g, serum albumin: 2.5 g/dl, microhematuria (16–20 red blood cells/high power field), low C4 (10 mg/dl), and low normal C3 (78 mg/dl). Antinuclear antibody, anti–double stranded DNA antibodies, hepatitis B and C serologies, HIV, antineutrophil cytoplasmic autoantibody, and rheumatoid factor were all negative or normal. A native kidney biopsy demonstrated membranoproliferative features, diffuse tubular degenerative changes, IgM-dominant glomerular staining by immunofluorescence, and scattered mesangial and subendothelial deposits by electron microscopy (
Supplementary Figure S1
). These findings were consistent with immune complex–mediated glomerulonephritis with membranoproliferative features and acute tubular injury. Although the precise cause could not be determined, the differential diagnosis included infection (probably viral) and cryoglobulinemia. One cryoglobulin test was negative, but this was not repeated.
Kidney function did not improve and 3-years later (at age of 46 years), the patient underwent a preemptive 4–human leukocyte antigens–mismatched kidney allograft from a deceased donor. No pretransplant circulating anti–human leukocyte antigen donor-specific antibodies (DSA) were detected. The patient received induction therapy with thymoglobulin and maintenance with tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil. The posttransplant course was relatively uneventful and both 4-month and 1-year protocol biopsies showed no significant pathologic findings.
Ten years posttransplantation, the patient presented with nephrotic syndrome in the setting of low tacrolimus levels. Laboratory work-up revealed serum creatinine: 0.9 mg/dl, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio: 11 g/g, serum albumin: 1.1 g/dl, and urine sediment with 3 to 5 red blood cells/high power field. An allograft biopsy was performed.
Kidney Allograft Biopsy
Sampling for light microscopy contained 9 glomeruli, of which 1 was near–globally sclerotic. The remaining glomeruli appeared mildly enlarged, with minimal mesangial hypercellularity, and occasional leukocytes within glomerular capillaries without overt glomerulitis. The glomerular basement membranes appeared thickened and showed scattered short double contours (
Figure 1
a). In addition, the sample demonstrated moderate peritubular capillaritis (
Figure 1
b), mild tubulointerstitial scarring without significant inflammation, and mild vascular sclerosis. Immunofluorescence showed diffuse C4d staining in peritubular capillaries (
Figure 1
c), and global finely granular staining for IgG (2+) (
Figure 1
d), kappa (1+), lambda (1+), C3 (trace), and C4d (2+) along glomerular capillaries. Ultrastructural evaluation revealed several granular subepithelial and rare mesangial and subendothelial deposits (
Figure 1
e). These findings were consistent with chronic-active ABMR and
de novo
MN. Immunoperoxidase staining for FAT1 revealed positive staining in glomerular capillaries (
Figure 1
f), consistent with FAT1-associated MN. Glomerular laser microdissection, followed by mass spectrometry analysis (LMD/MS),
3
showed increased spectral counts for FAT1 (
Supplementary Figure S2
A).
Figure 1
Histologic findings in the index allograft biopsy. (a) A glomerulus with thickened basement membranes, mild prominence of podocytes, and scattered short glomerular capillary wall duplication (arrowhead) (Jones methenamine silver, original magnification x400). (b) Dilated peritubular capillaries demonstrating margination of mononuclear leukocytes (Periodic Acid-Schiff, original magnification x400). (c) Positive C4d staining in peritubular capillaries (immunofluorescence, original magnification x400). (c) A glomerulus with finely granular IgG staining along glomerular capillaries (Immunofluorescence, original magnification x400). (e) Ultrastructural examination demonstrating subepithelial electron dense deposits (black arrowheads), subendothelial expansion by electron lucent material, and rare subendothelial electron dense deposits (white arrowhead) (Electron microscopy, original magnification x8000). (f) A glomerulus showing capillary wall staining for FAT1 [FAT1 immunoperoxidase stain, rabbit polyclonal primary antibody (Abcam, Waltham, MA), original magnification x400; inset showing negative FAT1 staining in glomerular capillaries of a case of PLA2R
+
membranous nephropathy, which was included only for comparison purposes].
De novo
DSAs were detected (DR53: 25,700 MFI, DQ5: 14,900 MFI) and the patient was treated with steroids, plasmapheresis, i.v. Ig, and rituximab. Unfortunately, the patient had persistent DSA and proteinuria, serum creatinine gradually increased to 3.9 mg/dl 14 months postbiopsy, and the patient resumed dialysis 4 months later.
To explore the temporal association of glomerular FAT1 levels with ABMR and
de novo
MN, LMD/MS was performed in the residual tissue from the native kidney biopsy and the 4-month protocol allograft biopsy and could not detect any FAT1 spectra (
Supplementary Figure S2
A).
To validate these observations, serial allograft biopsies from our second patient with FAT1-associated
de novo
MN, who was also described previously,
3
were assessed by LMD/MS. Similar to our index patient, there was no detectable spectra of FAT1 in the earlier biopsy before the development of ABMR (which was also associated with class-II DSA; DR51: 4,000 MFI) and
de novo
MN (
Supplementary Figure 2
SB). No sufficient residual to perform LMD/MS was noted in the index biopsy with rejection and
de novo
MN. However, residual tissue was available in 2 follow-up biopsies after treatment with steroids, plasmapheresis, i.v. Ig, and rituximab, and both biopsies showed abundant FAT1 spectra in the setting of persistence of MN and ABMR (
Supplementary Figure S2
B).
To explore whether ABMR by itself may cause increased glomerular FAT1 levels, 4 cases of C4d
+
ABMR without MN were assessed by LMD/MS. None of these cases showed detectable FAT1 spectra.
Discussion
MN can be associated with alloimmunity, either in the form of graft versus host disease following stem cell transplantation
5
or ABMR following kidney transplantation.
1
The negative PLA2R and the frequent detection of mesangial and/or subendoendothelial deposits
1
,
5
have led to the assumption that MN develops secondary to alloimmune response. This notion is further supported experimentally. For example, MN has been described following kidney transplantation in rats (LEW.1N donor kidney to BN recipient), where it tends to affect the kidney allograft while sparing the recipient's native kidney.
6
FAT1 is a large and heavily glycosylated protocadherin that is part of the podocyte slit diaphragm.
7
,
8
,
9
It has been identified as a target antigen in MN following hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.
8
Subsequently, we have shown accumulation of glomerular FAT1 in a subset of kidney transplant recipients with
de novo
MN associated with concurrent ABMR.
3
Using immunofluorescence, another study confirmed these findings and revealed persistence of positive FAT1 staining in follow-up biopsies from 3 patients showing ABMR and
de novo
MN and disappearance of FAT1 and weak IgG (1+) staining from another patient 1 month later, when DSA became undetectable.
4
However, that study relied solely on immunofluorescence FAT1 staining that was characterized as positive or negative and did not assess FAT1 in the biopsies preceding the development of ABMR or
de novo
MN.
In this report, we demonstrate that glomerular FAT1 changes from undetectable spectral counts by LMD/MS in the recipient native kidney and in donor allograft kidney before the development of ABMR and
de novo
MN, to elevated during the concurrent presence of both processes; and that elevated FAT1 spectral counts persisted during the active phase of these 2 diseases. In contrast, FAT1 was undetectable in active ABMR without MN. Together, these findings confirmed the association between FAT1 levels and ABMR in patients with
de novo
FAT1-associated MN and led us to speculate that alloimmune response may serve as a hit to expose cryptic epitope(s) on FAT1 in susceptible patients, which may then derive immune complex formation and FAT1 accumulation.
In summary, we have shown a temporal association between FAT1 and concurrent ABMR in patients with
de novo
FAT1-associated MN. Larger studies with detailed analyses of genetic predisposition in the donors and recipients are needed to foster our understanding of this process.
